title: Samuel's Farewell: A King Under God
summary: With Saul now confirmed as king, Samuel stands before all Israel, asks the people to testify that he has never cheated or oppressed them, and then reviews the LORD's faithfulness from Egypt to the present. He tells them their demand for a king was a great evil, calls down thunder and rain at the wheat harvest as a sign, and then comforts the frightened people: the LORD will not abandon them, and Samuel will not stop praying for them, provided king and people alike fear the LORD and serve him.
story: The long transition from the judges to the monarchy reaches its formal close here. Israel asked for a king in chapter 8, Saul was anointed in secret and chosen by lot in chapters 9 and 10, and he proved himself by rescuing Jabesh-gilead in chapter 11, after which the kingdom was renewed at Gilgal. Chapter 12 is Samuel's address at that ceremony. He does not retire from service (he keeps praying and teaching, and he will confront Saul twice in the chapters ahead), but he hands over the civil leadership that judges like him had carried. The chapter sets the terms by which the rest of the history will be judged: the monarchy can survive only if the king himself is a servant of Israel's true King.
historical:
The events belong to the late eleventh century BC, when Israel was a loose federation of tribes under pressure from the Philistines on the coastal plain and from Ammon and Moab east of the Jordan. Nahash, the Ammonite king named in verse 12, is the same ruler whose siege of Jabesh-gilead Saul broke in chapter 11. Exact dates for Saul's reign cannot be fixed; many historians place it roughly between 1050 and 1010 BC, but the chronology of this period is uncertain, and the text itself gives few anchors.

Samuel's review of history compresses the book of Judges into a few lines. Sisera and Hazor recall Judges 4 and 5; the Philistines and the king of Moab recall the oppressions in Judges 3 and 10 to 16. Jerubbaal is Gideon's other name (Judges 6:32). Where the BSB has Barak, the traditional Hebrew text reads Bedan, a name not otherwise known as a judge; the BSB follows the Greek translation and the Syriac, which read Barak. Some ancient versions also read Samson instead of Samuel in verse 11. These are small textual questions, and they don't change the point of the speech.
cultural:
Samuel's opening challenge is the language of a court. He calls the LORD and the anointed king as witnesses, lists the typical abuses of a powerful man (taking an ox or donkey, cheating, oppression, bribes that make a judge close his eyes), and invites anyone to bring a claim. It deliberately echoes the warning of 8:11-17, where Samuel said a king would take and take. The contrast is sharp: the old judge took nothing, and the new king will be tempted to take everything.

The sign in verses 16 to 18 would have struck an Israelite farmer hard. The wheat harvest came in late spring and early summer, in the dry season, when rain in the land of Israel is almost unknown and could ruin grain lying cut in the fields. Thunder and rain at that moment were plainly not ordinary weather. In a land where Baal was worshiped as the storm god who gave rain, the sign also said who actually commands the sky. The phrase “worthless things” in verse 21 renders a word used in Genesis 1:2 for the formless earth, and here it means idols: empty, unable to deliver.
literary: The chapter is a covenant speech, one of several farewell addresses that mark turning points in Israel's history (Moses in Deuteronomy, Joshua in Joshua 23 and 24). It follows a familiar pattern: a review of God's saving acts, a charge with a conditional promise and warning, a sign, and a renewed commitment. It is built as a trial in three movements. First, Samuel is cleared (verses 1 to 5). Then the LORD's righteous acts are laid out and the people are shown to be in the wrong (verses 6 to 15). Then the sign convicts them, and Samuel turns from prosecutor to intercessor (verses 16 to 25). The two conditional sentences in verses 14 and 15 sit at the center, and the final verse repeats the warning so that the chapter ends with weight rather than reassurance.

outline.t: Samuel's integrity attested before the LORD and his anointed
The LORD's righteous acts and Israel's repeated forgetting
The conditions: king and people must follow the LORD
Thunder and rain at the wheat harvest
Do not be afraid: Samuel's promise to pray and teach

doctrines.note: Samuel insists that “the LORD your God was your king” even when Israel asked for a human one. The monarchy is allowed, but only as a kingship under God; the king is judged by the same covenant as everyone else.

Samuel treats ceasing to pray for the people as a sin against the LORD. Intercession is not an optional extra for a leader but part of the office, and it continues even after the people have rejected his leadership.

The LORD will not abandon his people “for the sake of His great name,” because he chose to make them his own. The covenant rests on God's commitment, yet it still carries real conditions and real warnings for those inside it.

words.note: Mashiach, anointed. Used twice here of Saul, the king set apart by having oil poured on his head (10:1). The word describes an office, not yet a future figure, but it is the root of the title Messiah, and the story of Israel's anointed kings is where that hope begins to take shape.

Tsedaqah, righteousness. In verse 7 the plural means the LORD's righteous acts: his faithful deeds of rescue from Egypt onward. Righteousness here is not an abstract quality but God doing right by his people, which is why the speech can use it as evidence in a trial.

Tohu, formlessness or emptiness. The same word describes the earth as formless in Genesis 1:2. In verse 21 it is used twice for idols, the empty things that cannot profit or deliver. To turn from the LORD is to turn toward nothing.

christ: This chapter introduces a tension that runs through the rest of the Old Testament: Israel needs a king, but every human king is also a danger, and the LORD remains the true King. The anointed one in this chapter is Saul, and he will fail. The prophets later hope for a king from David's line who would rule in the fear of the LORD, and the New Testament names Jesus as that anointed one (the Christ). In him the tension is resolved rather than removed: the king is himself God with us, so obeying the king and obeying the LORD are no longer two things. Samuel's refusal to stop praying for a people who had rejected him also anticipates, by way of pattern rather than prediction, the one who “always lives to intercede” for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

hard.q: If asking for a king was a great evil, why did God give them one, and why does the Bible later celebrate David and the Messiah as kings?
hard.a: The difficulty is real, and the books of Samuel hold both sides on purpose. Deuteronomy 17:14-20 had already anticipated a king and set limits on him, so kingship as such was not forbidden. What Samuel condemns is the motive: Israel wanted a king “like all the other nations” (8:5) and, when Nahash threatened, turned to a human ruler instead of the LORD who had delivered them again and again. Some scholars see two strands in 1 Samuel, one favorable to monarchy and one critical of it, placed side by side by an editor. Others read the tension as a single deliberate argument. Either way, the resulting picture is consistent: a king is good only when he is himself under God's rule. God grants the request, turns it toward his own purpose, and later promises David an everlasting house. The sin lay in the demand, not in the office.

questions: Samuel could say publicly that he had never cheated anyone. What would it take for leaders you know, or for you, to be able to say the same?
Israel wanted a visible king when an invisible God felt too little protection. Where are you tempted to trust something you can see more than the God who has already delivered you?
Samuel called prayerlessness a sin against the LORD. Who in your life is easy to stop praying for, and why?
